newsitem.title: USA: Coverage assured under new health insurance law.
newsitem.headline: Coverage assured under new health insurance law.

text.p: If your company has a health insurance plan, it's in your best interest as an employee to get a certificate showing you're covered.

Under a new law that makes workplace health insurance portable, which took effect June 1, if you change jobs you're allowed to go from one company's health plan to another company's health plan with full coverage even if you have a pre-existing medical condition.
But you'll need that certificate as proof to show to your new employer that you were covered at your old job. You may also request certificates of coverage for your spouse and dependent children.

"I think quite frankly a lot of employers aren't issuing these certificates because there was not enough time to get their act together," said Rich Stover, of Buck Consultants, an employee benefits consulting firm based in Secaucus, N.J.
"Every employer but the Federal government is covered," Stover said, but "many small employers are not even aware of the change.
"Employees are largely ignorant of this new law and must be made aware of it starting now or they might lose coverage," Stover added.

Prior to enactment last year of the Health Insurance Portability And Accountability Act (HIPAA), if you switched jobs your new employer's plan could require you to wait a year before covering a pre-existing medical condition.

HIPAA amends COBRA, the Consolidated Budget Reconciliation Act of 1985. Under COBRA, employees who left a job often paid for coverage in their old plan for up to 18 months either because they had no new job or because their new employer's plan wouldn't cover a pre-existing medical problem.
Since a new employer now usually will have to pay for any pre-existing medical problem, workers who change jobs no longer have to pay into their old health plans for COBRA coverage.

"If you're switching jobs," Stover said, "and you had more than 12 months of (health insurance) coverage at your previous job, your new employer cannot limit coverage at all for pre-existing conditions."

If you were covered at your previous job, say, for three months, your new employer would have to subtract that time from the period in which the new health plan could deny you coverage under a pre-existing condition clause, Stover said.
Health plans can still have such clauses but employers cannot deny coverage to new hires longer than 12 months and may not withhold maternity benefits for any period of time.
Prior to HIPAA, Stover said, "It was real common for an employer to tell a new worker 'We won't cover your dependent until they get out of the hospital.' They can't do that any more."

If you switch jobs but choose to buy insurance other than through your new employer's health plan, the certificate will help you obtain coverage with no pre-existing condition exclusion. For further information on this point, contact your State insurance department.
According to HIPAA, an employer must inform a new employee if the company health plan has a pre-existing condition clause.

Employers, though, "might make employees pay more for health coverage who smoke or who don't participate in a wellness programme," Stover said. "It's a grey area. They (Federal government) don't have full regulations yet."

Aven Kerr, senior vice president for human resources of NovaCare, a rehabilitation therapy company based in King of Prussia, Pa., said HIPAA "allows employers to focus on recruiting people without focusing on the health care issue, and allows employees to move to more attractive jobs without losing health care coverage or benefits."
Kerr said that NovaCare's 17,000 employees will use their medical insurance cards as proof of coverage.
Buck Consultant's Stover predicted HIPAA will be a hassle for employers because if a new hire does not have a certificate the new employer must help the worker get one from the previous employer.

"The new law alone won't really increase employers' health care costs," Stover said. "What could induce employers to drop plans is the water-torture effect. Here's one more law to be aware of. The administrative cost could cause some employers to say 'No more'" to health plans.
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
